title: Competence, Current USP Standards, the Duty to Compound, Confidentiality and the Compounded-Preparation Label
topic: Professional practice / General practice standards in 247 CMR 9.01(3), (4), (15) and (16), and the compounded-preparation label and pharmacist telephone line in M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 21
subtopic: Practice within the pharmacist's education, training and experience and within the recognized pharmacist scope of practice under 247 CMR 9.01(4); adherence to the most current standards established by each chapter of the United States Pharmacopeia under 247 CMR 9.01(3), with the statutory USP duty of pharmacies licensed under M.G.L. c. 112, ss. 39G, 39H and 39I; the limit on refusing to compound simple or moderate non-sterile preparations customary to the community needs under 247 CMR 9.01(15), with the Board waiver under 247 CMR 14.01 and the non-sterile compounding expectation in Board Policy 2023-07; the licensee's duty to maintain patient confidentiality and protect confidential information under 247 CMR 9.01(16); and the compounded drug preparation label, the pharmacist telephone line and its institutional inpatient exception under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 21
learning_objectives: State the two cumulative limbs of 247 CMR 9.01(4) and explain why neither training nor an employer's direction can supply the recognized-scope limb.

Explain how 247 CMR 9.01(3) makes United States Pharmacopeia standards binding, what the words most current mean when a chapter is revised, and what the words unless otherwise regulated by the Board do and do not displace.

Recognise that pharmacies licensed under M.G.L. c. 112, ss. 39G, 39H and 39I carry a statutory duty to adhere to the most current USP standards in their licensed compounding, from which the Board's regulations for them may not exempt them.

Decide whether 247 CMR 9.01(15) reaches a compounding request by testing whether the preparation is non-sterile, simple or moderate, and customary to the community needs, using Board Policy 2023-07 as guidance on where complex non-sterile compounding begins.
Apply the two exceptions in 247 CMR 9.01(15), including who signs a petition for a Board waiver under 247 CMR 14.01, what the Board must find and when a waiver expires.

Separate the duty to maintain patient confidentiality from the duty to protect confidential information under 247 CMR 9.01(16), and state what the paragraph leaves undefined and the course that is safe on either reading of its silence about disclosures.
State which preparations must carry the sterile or non-sterile compounded drug preparation label under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 21, who affixes it, and why it is in addition to the ordinary label.
Identify the pharmacies that owe the s. 21 pharmacist telephone line, its staffing and placement requirements, and the narrow institutional inpatient exception that disapplies it.

orientation.text: 247 CMR 9.01 is the Board of Registration in Pharmacy's list of general practice standards. Four of its paragraphs are taught here: paragraph (3) on current United States Pharmacopeia standards, paragraph (4) on practising within competence and scope, paragraph (15) on refusing to compound, and paragraph (16) on confidentiality. Each is a single sentence that turns on a handful of words, so each rewards exact reading. Paragraph (4) is addressed to a pharmacist. Paragraphs (3), (15) and (16) are addressed to a licensee, a word 247 CMR 9.01 does not define; read in its ordinary sense it reaches whoever holds a licence or registration issued by the Board, a pharmacy as well as an individual, and the safe course is to treat every such holder as bound. The section also teaches the label that M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 21 requires on a compounded preparation and the pharmacist telephone line it requires of certain compounding pharmacies. The other paragraphs of 247 CMR 9.01 are taught elsewhere: paragraphs (1), (2), (5), (9) to (14) and (18) to (21), together with the advertising provision in 247 CMR 9.03 and the recovery and monitoring program, with the conduct standards for licensees; paragraphs (6) and (7) with returns, recalls and product integrity; paragraph (8) with the security of controlled stock; and paragraph (17) with the pharmacy internship.

Paragraph (4) provides that a pharmacist shall practice pharmacy within the scope of his or her education, training, and experience and within the recognized pharmacist scope of practice. The two limbs are joined by and, so an act has to satisfy both. The first limb is personal: it is measured by what this pharmacist's own education, training and experience cover. The second is professional: it asks whether the act lies within the recognized pharmacist scope of practice at all, a phrase 247 CMR 9.01 does not define. Neither limb can do the other's work. However skilled a pharmacist is, training and experience cannot carry an act that lies outside the recognized pharmacist scope of practice into it, and an act squarely within the profession's scope is still outside paragraph (4) for a pharmacist whose education, training and experience do not extend to it. Because the paragraph measures the first limb by the pharmacist's own preparation and the second by what is recognized for pharmacists, an employer's direction, a pharmacy's internal protocol or a colleague's confidence supplies neither. What Massachusetts law authorizes pharmacists to do in particular services, and on what conditions, is taught in the sections on those services, such as administration, collaborative drug therapy management and contraception, and is not settled by paragraph (4).

Three further points keep paragraph (4) in proportion. It does not say how education, training and experience combine for an act a pharmacist has been educated and trained to perform but has not yet performed, and reading experience as a separate precondition for every act would leave no pharmacist able to do anything for the first time. What the words plainly exclude is an act for which the pharmacist has neither training nor experience, and the safe course short of that is to undertake an act only when the pharmacist's education and training actually cover it. The paragraph also creates no documentation requirement and no Board authorization procedure of its own: the test is the pharmacist's actual preparation and the act's place within the recognized scope, not a certificate issued for the purpose. And it is addressed to a pharmacist. Pharmacy interns and pharmacy technicians work within limits that are taught with those roles, and the grounds on which the Board may discipline a licensee are taught in the section on grounds for Board discipline.

Paragraph (3) is the regulation that makes United States Pharmacopeia standards binding on a Massachusetts licensee: unless otherwise regulated by the Board, a licensee shall adhere to the most current standards established by each chapter of the United States Pharmacopeia (USP). Four features of the sentence do the work. Shall adhere makes the standards mandatory, not advisory. Each chapter draws no line between one chapter and another, so the duty is not confined to compounding or to any single chapter; what a given chapter requires is found in the USP text itself, which this section does not teach. Most current fixes the version, so the duty follows the standards as they currently stand rather than an edition the pharmacy bought, printed or trained on. And unless otherwise regulated by the Board makes the duty give way where the Board has regulated a point otherwise, so that on that point the licensee follows the Board's regulation. The paragraph names the United States Pharmacopeia and its chapters; it does not mention the National Formulary. Board Policy 2023-07, in its overview of non-sterile compounding, states as guidance that licensees are expected to adhere to the USP, but the obligation itself comes from the regulation.

What paragraph (3) says about a revised standard is carried entirely by the words most current. It names no edition, no official or effective date, no transition period and no grace period, and it does not tie the duty to an inspection, a renewal or the pharmacy's own purchasing cycle. Read in their ordinary sense, those words mean that once a chapter has been revised the revised standard is the most current one, and working to the superseded version no longer satisfies the paragraph; nothing in 247 CMR 9.01(3) preserves an earlier version for a licensee who has not caught up. The paragraph does not itself say at what moment a revision becomes the most current standard, so the safe course is to follow revisions as they are published and to work to each revised standard from the time it is in effect, rather than choosing a later date for convenience.

The displacement words need two cautions. The first is that they operate only where the Board has regulated a point otherwise. Silence in the Board's regulations leaves the USP standard binding, so the absence of a Massachusetts regulation on a subject is a reason to look to the USP, not a reason to treat a chapter as optional. The second is that they qualify the duty paragraph (3) imposes and do not reach a duty imposed by statute. M.G.L. c. 112, ss. 39G, 39H and 39I provide for the retail sterile compounding, retail complex non-sterile compounding and institutional sterile compounding pharmacy licences. Each provides that a pharmacy so licensed shall adhere to the most current standards established by USP, all chapters, when engaging in any form of the sterile or complex non-sterile compounding its licence concerns, and shall also adhere to the additional regulations the Board promulgates under subsection (c) of that section; and each provides that no such regulation shall exempt the pharmacy from compliance with the most current USP standards. In those statutes USP is a defined term: M.G.L. c. 112, s. 39D defines it, for s. 39D and ss. 36E to 42D, as the current edition of the United States Pharmacopeia and the National Formulary, whereas paragraph (3) supplies its own short form for the United States Pharmacopeia alone. For those pharmacies, in their licensed compounding, the Board's regulations add to current USP standards rather than replacing them. How those licences are obtained, inspected and renewed, and how hazardous drugs are handled, are taught with compounding operations.

Paragraph (15) makes compounding something a licensee may not simply decline, within limits the paragraph sets for itself: a licensee may not refuse to compound simple or moderate non-sterile compounded preparations customary to the community needs except upon extenuating circumstances or by a waiver of Board regulation. Read the object before the exceptions. The prohibition reaches a preparation that is non-sterile, that is simple or moderate, and that is customary to the community needs, and all three descriptions have to fit. A sterile preparation is outside it. So is complex non-sterile compounding, a category M.G.L. c. 112, s. 39D defines and Massachusetts licenses separately, and so is a preparation that is not customary to the needs of the community. Outside does not mean forbidden: the paragraph simply does not address refusing those requests, and whether a pharmacy may make them, and under which licence, is taught with compounding operations. Paragraph (15) does not define simple or moderate. The Board's Policy 2023-07 on non-sterile compounding, which is guidance rather than regulation, draws its working line at complex: it states that, except for complex non-sterile compounding, all pharmacies licensed by the Board are expected to engage in non-sterile compounding in accordance with Board regulations, and it gives as examples of complex non-sterile compounding, in a list it says is not all inclusive, the compounding of NIOSH drug containing preparations or other hazardous agents, the use of complex calculations, and the preparation of dosage forms including capsules, suppositories, troches, transdermal and sublingual dosage forms, tablets and modified-release preparations.

The Board's policy also helps decide whether a request is a compounding request at all. It states that simple reconstitution of FDA approved, conventionally manufactured non-sterile drug products in accordance with manufacturer package insert instructions is not considered compounding, and that adding flavoring agents to conventionally manufactured non-sterile drug products is. The policy's statement does not repeat the regulation's qualifiers, simple or moderate and customary to the community needs, and it is an expectation stated in guidance, while the prohibition on refusing is the regulation's. A question about what a licensee may not do is therefore answered from 247 CMR 9.01(15), and the policy shows where the Board draws the line between complex non-sterile compounding and the rest. Beside that expectation, 247 CMR 9.19(1)(g) and (j) require a pharmacy to maintain on the pharmacy premises the equipment necessary to perform simple and moderate non-sterile compounding and a designated compounding area for simple and moderate non-sterile compounding. 247 CMR 9.19(24) disapplies both requirements to institutional sterile compounding pharmacies, and 247 CMR 9.19(23) disapplies the designated compounding area to non-resident pharmacies.

Paragraph (15) states two exceptions. The first is extenuating circumstances, a phrase it does not define. In ordinary usage a circumstance extenuates when it lies outside the ordinary course of business and makes compounding the particular preparation impracticable while it lasts. A preference, a business decision to stop compounding, ordinary workload, or the fact that another pharmacy would make the preparation describes nothing of that kind, and treating any of them as extenuating would let the exception swallow the prohibition. That is a reading rather than a definition, so the safe course is to rely on the exception only for a circumstance the licensee could describe and justify if asked. The second exception is a waiver of Board regulation, which is the Board's to grant. Under 247 CMR 14.01, unless otherwise prohibited by law, the Board may waive compliance with a 247 CMR requirement if it finds that a compelling public interest would be served, that the petitioner's adherence would be impractical and unduly burdensome, and that there are sufficient safeguards to protect the public health, welfare and safety without compliance. The petition is made on a form supplied by the Board and is completed and signed by the current Manager of Record on behalf of a licensed pharmacy, or by the proposed Manager of Record on behalf of an applicant; the Board may require the applicant to appear personally before acting, and a waiver granted after June 30, 2013 expires on the fifth anniversary of the date it was granted. Where neither exception applies, what paragraph (15) requires is that the licensee not refuse. It adds no duty to refer, notify or record, and it offers no alternative, such as sending the patient to another pharmacy, that discharges it.

Paragraph (16) provides that a licensee shall maintain patient confidentiality and protect a patient's confidential information. The sentence carries two duties, and each can fail without the other. Maintaining confidentiality is broken by a disclosure: information passed to someone with no entitlement to it. Protecting confidential information is affirmative, and on the ordinary meaning of protect it is broken by leaving the information exposed, whether or not anyone is shown to have read it: filled prescriptions with labels facing the waiting area, a screen or printed list of patients in view of the queue, or records left where people not entitled to them can reach them. A pharmacy that locks its records away but hands a patient's medication history to someone with no entitlement fails the first duty; a pharmacist who never tells anyone anything but leaves the information on display fails the second. A secure channel is a measure of protection, not an authority to disclose, so encrypting a transmission to a recipient with no entitlement does not keep the patient's confidence.

The paragraph defines neither patient confidentiality nor confidential information, and it states no exceptions: it names no permitted recipient, no form of patient authorization and no disclosure required by law. Two things fix at least part of its reach. The Board's own regulations call the patient profile that a pharmacist and pharmacy must maintain under 247 CMR 9.16(7) a confidential patient profile (247 CMR 9.16(8) disapplies 9.16 to institutional sterile compounding pharmacies), and in ordinary usage what a pharmacy knows about a patient because he or she is its patient, including identity, prescriptions and medication history, is the patient's confidential information; the safe course is to treat all of it as within the paragraph. The silence about disclosures is genuinely open to two readings. On one, any disclosure breaches the duty unless another provision of law requires or permits it. On the other, maintaining patient confidentiality carries its ordinary meaning, under which telling the patient, or disclosing at the patient's direction, breaks no confidence. The course that is safe on either reading is to disclose a patient's confidential information only to the patient, with the patient's authorization, or where a specific provision of law requires or permits that disclosure to that recipient, and to treat a requester's stated purpose, an employment relationship, a secure channel or convenience as supplying none of those. The federal privacy rules are taught in a later section; where federal and Massachusetts requirements both reach a disclosure, the licensee must satisfy both, which means following the stricter. The privacy of the patient consultation area is taught with patient counseling, the contents of the patient profile with prospective drug review, and prescription monitoring program data with prescription validity and opioid safety.

M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 21 is best known for the dispensing label, and its fourth paragraph applies the section's labeling provisions to the compounding and dispensing of drugs on the oral, electronic or written prescription of a licensed and registered prescriber under section 9; that general label is taught with the dispensing label and record. The same paragraph then adds a label of its own for compounded preparations: all drug preparations compounded, made or formulated by a pharmacy licensed by the board of registration in pharmacy shall have affixed to their container by the compounding pharmacy a label notifying prescribed users and practitioners that the drug is either a sterile or non-sterile compounded drug preparation. Three features decide most questions. Its reach is every preparation compounded, made or formulated by a pharmacy the Board licenses, sterile or non-sterile, simple or complex, so a drug store that adds a flavoring agent to a conventionally manufactured suspension, which the Board's policy treats as compounding, owes it as much as a sterile compounding pharmacy does. The duty rests on the compounding pharmacy and attaches to the container. And the label has to tell prescribed users and practitioners which of the two the preparation is, sterile or non-sterile. The sentence states no exception, and the compounded-preparation label is in addition to the ordinary label elements rather than a substitute for them.

The fifth paragraph adds a telephone line, and it reaches fewer pharmacies. It applies to all pharmacies engaged in sterile or complex non-sterile compounding and licensed under sections 39G to 39I, inclusive, of chapter 112, the sections that provide for the retail sterile, retail complex non-sterile and institutional sterile compounding pharmacy licences; both conditions, engagement and licensure, are in the text. Such a pharmacy shall provide a telephone number to foster communication between patients in the commonwealth and a pharmacist employed by the pharmacy who has access to the patient's records. The phone shall be staffed during regular hours of operation every day and not less than 56 hours per week. The two conditions are joined by and, so a pharmacy whose regular hours add up to fewer than 56 in a week still owes at least 56 hours of staffing, and the safe course is to staff the line on every day of the week. The number shall be affixed to the drug's container, alongside the label notifying prescribed users and practitioners that the drug is a compounded drug preparation. A line that cannot put a caller in touch with a pharmacist employed by the pharmacy who has access to the patient's records does not do what the paragraph describes. The paragraph does not say whether the number belongs only on a covered pharmacy's sterile or complex non-sterile preparations or on every compounded preparation it labels; because it speaks of the drug's container without narrowing it, the safe course for a covered pharmacy is to place the number beside the compounded drug preparation label on all of them. The paragraph names only pharmacies licensed under M.G.L. c. 112, ss. 39G to 39I, and says nothing of the non-resident sterile and complex non-sterile compounding pharmacy licenses that 247 CMR 6.02(5) and (6) require of a pharmacy outside Massachusetts shipping those preparations into Massachusetts and that 247 CMR 6.09 provides for, so its text does not say whether a non-resident compounding pharmacy owes the line; because 247 CMR 9.20 requires a non-resident pharmacy to comply with all Massachusetts laws and regulations governing the practice of pharmacy when filling, dispensing, or shipping medications into Massachusetts, unless otherwise specified, the safe course for such a pharmacy is to provide the line as the paragraph describes.

One exception is written into the fifth paragraph, and it is narrow. The paragraph shall not apply to an institutional pharmacy licensed pursuant to section 39I of chapter 112 if the sterile drug preparation compounded by such pharmacy is to be administered to an individual admitted as an inpatient within the same hospital. Every element has to be present: a licence under s. 39I, a sterile preparation that pharmacy compounded, administration to an individual admitted as an inpatient, and the same hospital. A retail compounding pharmacy, a complex non-sterile preparation, a preparation for an outpatient and a preparation for an inpatient of a different hospital all fall outside it. And the exception disapplies only the telephone paragraph. The compounded drug preparation label sits in the paragraph before it, which states no exception, so a sterile preparation for an inpatient of the same hospital needs no telephone number but still needs its label identifying it as a sterile compounded drug preparation.

worked_examples.scenario: A pharmacist who worked for years in another health profession before pharmacy school is asked by her manager to perform, for a patient at the counter, a procedure her earlier career trained her to do well but that is not within the recognized pharmacist scope of practice. The same afternoon a newly hired colleague is told to provide a service that is within the recognized pharmacist scope of practice, although he has never been trained in it and has never performed it. The manager says both are covered because the pharmacy's protocol lists them.
steps: Read 247 CMR 9.01(4) as two limbs joined by and: a pharmacist shall practice pharmacy within the scope of his or her education, training, and experience, and within the recognized pharmacist scope of practice.

Test the first pharmacist on the professional limb. On the facts the procedure is not within the recognized pharmacist scope of practice, and training acquired in another profession cannot put it there, however skilled she is.

Test the colleague on the personal limb. The service is within the recognized pharmacist scope of practice, but he has neither training nor experience in it, so it is outside the scope of his education, training, and experience.

Test the protocol. Paragraph (4) measures competence by the pharmacist's own education, training and experience and measures scope by what is recognized for pharmacists; neither limb refers to an employer's direction or a pharmacy's internal protocol, so the protocol supplies neither.

Keep the particular services out of the analysis. Which services Massachusetts law authorizes pharmacists to provide, and on what conditions, is taught in the sections on those services and is not decided by paragraph (4).
worked_examples.resolution: Neither pharmacist should proceed: the first fails the recognized-scope limb and the second fails the competence limb. The error the scenario invites is treating either limb as enough on its own, and treating the pharmacy's protocol as if it could supply the limb that is missing.

worked_examples.scenario: A drug store pharmacy that also holds a retail sterile compounding licence learns that a USP chapter it relies on has been revised. Its Manager of Record proposes to keep working to the superseded version until the pharmacy's next licence renewal, noting that 247 CMR 9.01(3) names no date for switching. She adds that if the Board ever adopts a regulation for sterile compounding pharmacies on the same subject, the pharmacy will be free of the USP chapter altogether, including in its sterile compounding.
steps: Start with the text. 247 CMR 9.01(3) provides that, unless otherwise regulated by the Board, a licensee shall adhere to the most current standards established by each chapter of the United States Pharmacopeia.

Apply the words most current. The paragraph names no edition, date, transition period or grace period and does not tie the duty to renewal or inspection, so once the revised standard is the most current one the superseded version no longer satisfies the paragraph.

Note what the paragraph leaves open. It does not say at what moment a revision becomes the most current standard, so the safe course is to follow the revision and work to it from the time it is in effect rather than choosing a later date.
Apply the displacement words to the pharmacy's work generally. Where the Board has regulated a point otherwise, paragraph (3) gives way on that point and the Board's regulation governs it.

Apply the licence statute to the sterile compounding. Under M.G.L. c. 112, s. 39G(a)(4) a retail sterile compounding pharmacy shall adhere to the most current standards established by USP, all chapters, when engaging in any form of sterile compounding, and under s. 39G(c)(4) no regulation the Board promulgates for those pharmacies shall exempt the pharmacy from compliance with them.
worked_examples.resolution: The superseded version stops satisfying 247 CMR 9.01(3) once the revision is the most current standard, and in its sterile compounding the pharmacy cannot be freed of current USP standards by the regulations the Board makes for its licence category. The errors the scenario invites are reading silence about dates as permission to wait, and treating the displacement words in a regulation as reaching a duty the statute imposes.

worked_examples.scenario: A parent brings a prescription for a conventionally manufactured antibiotic suspension to a drug store pharmacy and asks for a flavoring agent to be added, a request pharmacies in the community routinely fill. The pharmacist on duty says the pharmacy has stopped compounding and that the pharmacy across the street will do it. Later the same day the pharmacy, which holds no complex non-sterile compounding licence, declines a prescription for compounded capsules.
steps: Classify the first request. Board Policy 2023-07, which is guidance, treats adding flavoring agents to conventionally manufactured non-sterile drug products as compounding, and flavoring is not among the policy's examples of complex non-sterile compounding.

Apply 247 CMR 9.01(15). A licensee may not refuse to compound simple or moderate non-sterile compounded preparations customary to the community needs, and a request pharmacies in the community routinely fill is customary to those needs.

Test the reasons against the two exceptions. A decision to stop compounding is a preference, not an extenuating circumstance on any ordinary reading; another pharmacy's willingness to do the work describes no circumstance affecting this licensee; and there is no Board waiver.
Note what the paragraph does not offer instead. It requires the licensee not to refuse, and it contains no referral option that discharges the duty.

Classify the second request. The Board's policy lists capsules among its examples of complex non-sterile compounding, a category M.G.L. c. 112, s. 39D defines and Massachusetts licenses separately, so on the Board's classification paragraph (15) does not reach it; whether this pharmacy may make capsules at all is a licensure question taught with compounding operations.
worked_examples.resolution: The first refusal is one 247 CMR 9.01(15) forbids; the second falls outside the paragraph on the Board's classification. The error the scenario invites is treating a referral to another pharmacy as a substitute for compounding, with a second error close behind it: assuming the duty reaches every compounding request, complex ones included.

worked_examples.scenario: A pharmacy's compounding area will be unusable for many months while its building is restored after flood damage. A staff pharmacist e-mails the Board that the pharmacy is taking a one-year waiver of the compounding requirement, and staff begin telling patients who ask for simple compounded preparations to go elsewhere. The Manager of Record has not seen the e-mail.
steps: Identify the paragraph and its two exceptions. Under 247 CMR 9.01(15) a licensee may not refuse to compound simple or moderate non-sterile compounded preparations customary to the community needs except upon extenuating circumstances or by a waiver of Board regulation.

Consider extenuating circumstances first. Flood damage that leaves a pharmacy with nowhere to compound lies outside the ordinary course of business and makes compounding impracticable while it lasts, which is what the phrase most naturally describes, although the paragraph defines no such term.

Turn to the waiver. Under 247 CMR 14.01, unless otherwise prohibited by law, the Board may waive a 247 CMR requirement if it finds a compelling public interest served by the waiver, adherence impractical and unduly burdensome, and sufficient safeguards to protect the public health, welfare and safety without compliance.

Check who may ask and how. The petition goes on a form supplied by the Board, completed and signed by the current Manager of Record on behalf of the licensed pharmacy, listing each requirement and explaining the public interest, the burden and the safeguards; the Board may require a personal appearance before acting.
Note the duration. A waiver granted after June 30, 2013 expires on the fifth anniversary of its grant, after which the pharmacy must comply unless the Board has granted a subsequent waiver.
worked_examples.resolution: The pharmacy has no waiver: a staff pharmacist's e-mail is not a petition, the Manager of Record signed nothing, and the Board has decided nothing. What can carry the pharmacy through the restoration is the extenuating-circumstances exception, on an ordinary reading for as long as the flood damage actually prevents compounding. The error the scenario invites is treating a waiver as a notice a licensee gives rather than a decision the Board makes.

worked_examples.scenario: An occupational health vendor working for a patient's employer faxes a pharmacy a request for the patient's dispensing history, enclosing no authorization from the patient and citing no law. The pharmacist sends the history to the vendor's secure fax line and logs the transmission. Meanwhile the pharmacy's pickup screen, which shows each waiting patient's name and drug, faces the queue, and the pharmacist's view is that no one has complained.
steps: Read the paragraph as two duties. Under 247 CMR 9.01(16) a licensee shall maintain patient confidentiality and protect a patient's confidential information.

Identify the information. The paragraph defines neither term, but a patient's dispensing history and the names and drugs of waiting patients are what ordinary usage treats as a patient's confidential information, and the safe course is to treat them as within the paragraph.

Apply the duty to maintain confidentiality to the fax. The paragraph lists no permitted disclosures, and on the course that is safe on either reading a disclosure needs the patient's authorization or a specific provision of law requiring or permitting it to that recipient; the vendor offered neither.
Reject the channel as an answer. A secure fax line and a transmission log protect the information in transit, but they do not make the vendor someone entitled to receive it.

Apply the duty to protect to the screen. Displaying names and drugs toward the queue leaves confidential information unprotected, and nothing in the paragraph makes that duty wait for a complaint or for proof that someone read the screen.
worked_examples.resolution: Both practices fail 247 CMR 9.01(16): the fax fails the duty to maintain patient confidentiality and the screen fails the duty to protect confidential information. The error the scenario invites is reading confidentiality as a single rule against careless talk, so that a logged, secure transmission looks compliant and an exposed screen looks harmless until someone objects.

worked_examples.scenario: An institutional pharmacy holding an institutional sterile compounding licence under M.G.L. c. 112, s. 39I compounds three sterile preparations in one morning: one to be administered to an inpatient on a ward of its own hospital, one for an outpatient to take home after a clinic visit, and one supplied for an inpatient of a different hospital. The pharmacy manager proposes to leave both the compounded-preparation label and the telephone number off the first, and to print on the other two the number of the pharmacy's purchasing office, which a buyer answers on weekday business hours.
steps: Apply the label sentence to all three. Under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 21 all drug preparations compounded, made or formulated by a pharmacy licensed by the Board shall have affixed to their container by the compounding pharmacy a label notifying prescribed users and practitioners that the drug is either a sterile or non-sterile compounded drug preparation, and that sentence states no exception.
Confirm the telephone paragraph reaches this pharmacy. It is engaged in sterile compounding and licensed under s. 39I, which is within sections 39G to 39I, inclusive, of chapter 112.

Test each preparation against the exception. The telephone paragraph shall not apply to an institutional pharmacy licensed under s. 39I if the sterile drug preparation it compounded is to be administered to an individual admitted as an inpatient within the same hospital; the first preparation meets every element, while the outpatient's preparation and the preparation for another hospital's inpatient do not.

Test the proposed number. The line must foster communication between patients and a pharmacist employed by the pharmacy who has access to the patient's records, and it must be staffed during regular hours of operation every day and not less than 56 hours per week; a purchasing office answered by a buyer on weekday business hours meets none of those terms.
Place the number correctly. It is affixed to the drug's container alongside the compounded drug preparation label.
worked_examples.resolution: The first preparation needs its sterile compounded drug preparation label but no telephone number; the other two need the label and, beside it, a number that reaches a pharmacist employed by the pharmacy with access to the patient's records, staffed as the paragraph requires. The error the scenario invites is reading the inpatient exception as an exception to both compounded-preparation provisions, and as reaching any inpatient rather than an inpatient of the same hospital.

worked_examples.scenario: A drug store pharmacy that holds no sterile or complex non-sterile compounding licence adds a flavoring agent to a conventionally manufactured antibiotic suspension at a parent's request. The pharmacist prints the ordinary prescription label and adds nothing else, reasoning that the compounded-preparation label and the telephone number are both requirements for sterile compounding pharmacies.
steps: Decide whether the flavoring is compounding. Board Policy 2023-07, which is guidance, states that adding flavoring agents to conventionally manufactured non-sterile drug products is considered compounding.

Apply the label sentence of M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 21. All drug preparations compounded, made or formulated by a pharmacy licensed by the Board shall have affixed to their container by the compounding pharmacy a label notifying prescribed users and practitioners that the drug is either a sterile or non-sterile compounded drug preparation, and the sentence is not limited to sterile or complex compounding.
Choose the right description. The suspension is non-sterile, so the label identifies it as a non-sterile compounded drug preparation, in addition to the ordinary label elements.

Test the telephone paragraph separately. It reaches pharmacies engaged in sterile or complex non-sterile compounding and licensed under M.G.L. c. 112, ss. 39G to 39I, inclusive, and this pharmacy is neither engaged in that compounding nor so licensed, so the paragraph does not require the line of it.
worked_examples.resolution: The pharmacy owes the non-sterile compounded drug preparation label but not the telephone line. The error the scenario invites is treating the two s. 21 provisions as one, so that a pharmacy correctly outside the telephone paragraph wrongly concludes it is outside the label duty as well.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Which two limbs does 247 CMR 9.01(4) require a pharmacist's practice to satisfy?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Practice within the scope of his or her education, training, and experience, and within the recognized pharmacist scope of practice. The limbs are joined by and, so both must be met.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: True or false: a pharmacist thoroughly trained in a procedure may perform it once the pharmacy's protocol lists it, even though it is not within the recognized pharmacist scope of practice.
retrieval_prompts.answer: False. Training speaks only to the personal limb of 247 CMR 9.01(4), and neither training nor a pharmacy protocol can bring an act within the recognized pharmacist scope of practice.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Under 247 CMR 9.01(3), a licensee shall adhere to ______ established by ______ of the United States Pharmacopeia, unless ______.
retrieval_prompts.answer: the most current standards; each chapter; otherwise regulated by the Board.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What transition period does 247 CMR 9.01(3) allow after a USP chapter is revised?
retrieval_prompts.answer: None is stated. The paragraph names no edition, date, transition period or grace period; the duty runs to the most current standards, so the superseded version no longer satisfies it once the revision is the most current standard.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: True or false: 247 CMR 9.01(3) binds a licensee to the United States Pharmacopeia and the National Formulary.
retrieval_prompts.answer: False as a statement of that paragraph. 247 CMR 9.01(3) names the United States Pharmacopeia and its chapters and does not mention the National Formulary. The National Formulary appears in the definition of USP in M.G.L. c. 112, s. 39D, which governs the compounding licence statutes.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Where the Board's regulations say nothing about a point a USP chapter addresses, what does 247 CMR 9.01(3) require?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Adherence to the most current USP standard on that point. The duty gives way only where the Board has regulated the point otherwise.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Can a regulation the Board promulgates for retail sterile compounding pharmacies under M.G.L. c. 112, s. 39G(c) exempt such a pharmacy from current USP standards in its sterile compounding?
retrieval_prompts.answer: No. Section 39G(a)(4) requires adherence to the most current standards established by USP, all chapters, when engaging in any form of sterile compounding, and s. 39G(c)(4) provides that no such regulation shall exempt the pharmacy from compliance with them. Sections 39H and 39I say the same for retail complex non-sterile and institutional sterile compounding pharmacies.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Name the three descriptions a preparation must fit before 247 CMR 9.01(15) forbids a licensee to refuse to compound it.
retrieval_prompts.answer: It must be non-sterile, simple or moderate, and customary to the community needs.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What are the two exceptions stated in 247 CMR 9.01(15)?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Extenuating circumstances, and a waiver of Board regulation.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: True or false: a pharmacy that declines a customary simple non-sterile compounding request but directs the patient to a pharmacy that will compound it has complied with 247 CMR 9.01(15).
retrieval_prompts.answer: False. The paragraph forbids refusing, subject only to extenuating circumstances or a Board waiver, and it contains no referral option that discharges the duty. Another pharmacy's willingness describes no circumstance affecting this licensee.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: According to Board Policy 2023-07, which non-sterile compounding are all Board-licensed pharmacies expected to engage in, and what kind of authority is that statement?
retrieval_prompts.answer: All non-sterile compounding except complex non-sterile compounding, in accordance with Board regulations. It is Board guidance; the prohibition on refusing to compound is the regulation in 247 CMR 9.01(15).

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Give three dosage forms Board Policy 2023-07 lists as examples of complex non-sterile compounding, and say how complete the list is.
retrieval_prompts.answer: Any three of transdermal dosage forms, capsules, suppositories, troches, lollipops, sublingual dosage forms, tablets, tablet triturates, modified-release preparations and other dosage forms intended to deliver systemic effects. The policy says the list is not all inclusive.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Who completes and signs a petition to waive a 247 CMR requirement for a licensed pharmacy, and what three things must the Board find before granting it?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The current Manager of Record, on a form supplied by the Board. The Board must find that a compelling public interest would be served, that the petitioner's adherence would be impractical and unduly burdensome, and that there are sufficient safeguards to protect the public health, welfare and safety without compliance.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A Board waiver was granted on March 3, 2024. When does it expire, and what happens then?
retrieval_prompts.answer: On March 3, 2029, the fifth anniversary of its grant. The pharmacy must then comply with all 247 CMR requirements unless the Board has granted a subsequent waiver, for which it may petition in anticipation of, or following, expiration.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: True or false: a pharmacist who never discloses any patient information to anyone has satisfied 247 CMR 9.01(16).
retrieval_prompts.answer: False. The paragraph also requires the licensee to protect a patient's confidential information, and leaving that information exposed fails that duty without any disclosure.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Which disclosures does 247 CMR 9.01(16) expressly permit?
retrieval_prompts.answer: None. It lists no permitted recipient or disclosure and defines neither patient confidentiality nor confidential information. The course safe on either reading is to disclose only to the patient, with the patient's authorization, or where a specific provision of law requires or permits that disclosure to that recipient.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Which pharmacy record does 247 CMR 9.16(7) describe as confidential?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The patient profile a pharmacist and pharmacy must maintain for each patient to whom a prescription is dispensed, which 247 CMR 9.16(7) calls a confidential patient profile. Under 247 CMR 9.16(8) that requirement does not apply to institutional sterile compounding pharmacies.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 21, which preparations must carry a label identifying them as sterile or non-sterile compounded drug preparations, and who affixes it?
retrieval_prompts.answer: All drug preparations compounded, made or formulated by a pharmacy licensed by the Board; the compounding pharmacy affixes the label to their container, notifying prescribed users and practitioners.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: The s. 21 telephone line must be staffed ______ and not less than ______ hours per week, and it fosters communication between patients and ______.
retrieval_prompts.answer: during regular hours of operation every day; 56; a pharmacist employed by the pharmacy who has access to the patient's records.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Which pharmacies owe the s. 21 telephone line?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Pharmacies engaged in sterile or complex non-sterile compounding and licensed under M.G.L. c. 112, ss. 39G to 39I, inclusive, the sections that provide for the retail sterile, retail complex non-sterile and institutional sterile compounding pharmacy licences.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: True or false: an institutional sterile compounding pharmacy may leave the compounded drug preparation label off a sterile preparation to be administered to an inpatient of its own hospital.
retrieval_prompts.answer: False. The inpatient exception disapplies only the telephone paragraph of s. 21. The label sentence states no exception, so the preparation still carries its sterile compounded drug preparation label.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Does a drug store pharmacy with no sterile or complex non-sterile compounding licence need the s. 21 telephone line when it adds a flavoring agent to a conventionally manufactured suspension?
retrieval_prompts.answer: No; the telephone paragraph reaches only pharmacies engaged in sterile or complex non-sterile compounding and licensed under M.G.L. c. 112, ss. 39G to 39I. It does owe the non-sterile compounded drug preparation label, because Board Policy 2023-07 treats adding flavoring agents to conventionally manufactured non-sterile drug products as compounding.

quick_review.text: 247 CMR 9.01(4): a pharmacist shall practice pharmacy within the scope of his or her education, training, and experience and within the recognized pharmacist scope of practice; both limbs must be met.

Training and experience cannot enlarge the recognized pharmacist scope of practice, the recognized scope does not make an untrained pharmacist competent, and an employer's direction or internal protocol supplies neither limb.
247 CMR 9.01(3): unless otherwise regulated by the Board, a licensee shall adhere to the most current standards established by each chapter of the United States Pharmacopeia.
Most current means the standards as they currently stand; paragraph (3) names no edition, date, transition period or grace period, and it does not mention the National Formulary.
Where the Board has regulated a point otherwise, paragraph (3) gives way on that point; where the Board is silent, the USP standard binds.

Pharmacies licensed under M.G.L. c. 112, ss. 39G, 39H and 39I shall adhere to the most current standards established by USP, all chapters, in their licensed compounding, and no regulation the Board promulgates for them under subsection (c) shall exempt them.

247 CMR 9.01(15): a licensee may not refuse to compound simple or moderate non-sterile compounded preparations customary to the community needs except upon extenuating circumstances or by a waiver of Board regulation.

Paragraph (15) does not reach sterile preparations, complex non-sterile compounding or preparations not customary to the community needs, and where it applies it adds no referral, notice or record duty.

Board Policy 2023-07, as guidance, expects all Board-licensed pharmacies to engage in non-sterile compounding except complex non-sterile compounding, and lists capsules, suppositories and troches among its examples of complex, in a list it says is not all inclusive.

247 CMR 9.19(1)(g) and (j): a pharmacy shall maintain on the premises the equipment necessary to perform simple and moderate non-sterile compounding and a designated compounding area for it; 9.19(24) disapplies both to institutional sterile compounding pharmacies, and 9.19(23) disapplies the area to non-resident pharmacies.

Under 247 CMR 14.01 the Board may, unless otherwise prohibited by law, waive a 247 CMR requirement if it finds a compelling public interest, adherence impractical and unduly burdensome, and sufficient safeguards; the Manager of Record signs the petition, and a waiver granted after June 30, 2013 expires on the fifth anniversary of its grant.
247 CMR 9.01(16): a licensee shall maintain patient confidentiality and protect a patient's confidential information; either duty can fail without the other.

Paragraph (16) defines no terms and lists no permitted disclosures; the safe course is to disclose only to the patient, with the patient's authorization, or where a specific provision of law requires or permits that disclosure to that recipient.

M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 21: all drug preparations compounded, made or formulated by a pharmacy licensed by the Board carry a label, affixed by the compounding pharmacy, notifying prescribed users and practitioners that the drug is a sterile or non-sterile compounded drug preparation.

Pharmacies engaged in sterile or complex non-sterile compounding and licensed under M.G.L. c. 112, ss. 39G to 39I provide a telephone number reaching a pharmacist employed by the pharmacy with access to the patient's records, staffed during regular hours of operation every day and not less than 56 hours per week, and affixed beside the compounded-preparation label.

The telephone paragraph does not apply to an institutional pharmacy licensed under M.G.L. c. 112, s. 39I for a sterile preparation it compounded that is to be administered to an individual admitted as an inpatient within the same hospital; the compounded-preparation label still applies.

decision_logic.condition: A pharmacist is asked to perform an act.
decision_logic.action: Require a yes to both questions in 247 CMR 9.01(4): is the act within the recognized pharmacist scope of practice, and is it within this pharmacist's own education, training, and experience? An employer's direction or a pharmacy protocol answers neither question.

decision_logic.condition: The pharmacist's training covers the act, but the act is not within the recognized pharmacist scope of practice.
decision_logic.action: Decline it. Training bears only on the personal limb and cannot bring the act within the recognized scope.

decision_logic.condition: A USP chapter the licensee relies on has been revised.
decision_logic.action: Work to the revised standard from the time it is the most current one. 247 CMR 9.01(3) names no edition, date, transition period or grace period, so the safe course is to follow revisions as they are published rather than wait for an inspection or renewal.

decision_logic.condition: The Board has regulated a point that a USP chapter also addresses, and the two differ.
decision_logic.action: Under 247 CMR 9.01(3) follow the Board's regulation on that point. If the pharmacy holds a licence under M.G.L. c. 112, ss. 39G, 39H or 39I and the point arises in its licensed compounding, the statutory duty to adhere to the most current USP standards still applies, and the regulations the Board makes for those pharmacies may not exempt it, so comply with both.

decision_logic.condition: A compounding request is received and the licensee is inclined to decline it.
decision_logic.action: Classify the request first. If it is sterile, complex non-sterile, or not customary to the community needs, 247 CMR 9.01(15) does not reach it. If it is a simple or moderate non-sterile preparation customary to the community needs, the licensee may not refuse unless an exception applies. Use Board Policy 2023-07 as guidance on what counts as compounding and where complex non-sterile compounding begins.

decision_logic.condition: The reason offered for refusing is preference, a decision to stop compounding, ordinary workload, or another pharmacy's willingness to compound.
decision_logic.action: Do not treat it as an extenuating circumstance, and do not treat referral as compliance; compound the preparation.

decision_logic.condition: A genuine disruption prevents compounding for a time.
decision_logic.action: Paragraph (15) does not define extenuating circumstances, so rely on the exception only for a circumstance outside the ordinary course of business that the licensee could describe and justify, and only while it lasts.

decision_logic.condition: A pharmacy wants to be excused from a 247 CMR requirement, including paragraph (15), for a sustained period.
decision_logic.action: Petition the Board under 247 CMR 14.01 on the Board's form, completed and signed by the Manager of Record, with the contents 14.01(3) requires. A waiver exists only once the Board grants it, and a waiver granted after June 30, 2013 expires on the fifth anniversary of its grant.

decision_logic.condition: Someone other than the patient asks for a patient's information.
decision_logic.action: Disclose only with the patient's authorization or where a specific provision of law requires or permits that disclosure to that recipient; the requester's stated purpose, an employment relationship or a secure channel supplies neither.

decision_logic.condition: Patient information is visible or within reach in the pharmacy's ordinary workflow.
decision_logic.action: Correct the exposure. The duty to protect a patient's confidential information under 247 CMR 9.01(16) does not wait for a disclosure, a complaint or proof that anyone read it.

decision_logic.condition: A pharmacy licensed by the Board compounds, makes or formulates a drug preparation.
decision_logic.action: Affix to the container, in addition to the ordinary label elements, a label notifying prescribed users and practitioners that the drug is either a sterile or a non-sterile compounded drug preparation.

decision_logic.condition: The pharmacy is engaged in sterile or complex non-sterile compounding and licensed under M.G.L. c. 112, ss. 39G to 39I, inclusive.
decision_logic.action: Provide a telephone number that fosters communication between patients and a pharmacist employed by the pharmacy who has access to the patient's records, staffed during regular hours of operation every day and not less than 56 hours per week, and affix it to the container alongside the compounded drug preparation label.

decision_logic.condition: An institutional sterile compounding pharmacy's sterile preparation is going to an inpatient.
decision_logic.action: Confirm the licence is under M.G.L. c. 112, s. 39I, that the pharmacy compounded the sterile preparation, and that it is to be administered to an individual admitted as an inpatient within the same hospital. If every element is met, the telephone number is not required; the sterile compounded drug preparation label still is.

ma_vs_federal.text: 247 CMR 9.01(16) is a Massachusetts duty stated on its own terms and makes no reference to federal privacy law. The federal privacy rules are taught in a later section; where federal and Massachusetts requirements both reach a disclosure, the licensee must satisfy both, which means following the stricter.

exceptions.text: 247 CMR 9.01(3) applies unless otherwise regulated by the Board: where the Board has regulated a point otherwise, the Board's regulation governs that point.

The displacement words in 247 CMR 9.01(3) do not reach the statutory duty of pharmacies licensed under M.G.L. c. 112, ss. 39G, 39H and 39I to adhere to the most current USP standards in their licensed compounding, and no regulation the Board promulgates for those pharmacies under subsection (c) of those sections shall exempt them.

247 CMR 9.01(15) yields upon extenuating circumstances, a phrase it does not define; preference, ordinary workload or another pharmacy's willingness to compound does not describe one on an ordinary reading.

247 CMR 9.01(15) yields by a waiver of Board regulation. Under 247 CMR 14.01 the Board may, unless otherwise prohibited by law, waive a 247 CMR requirement if it finds a compelling public interest would be served, adherence would be impractical and unduly burdensome, and sufficient safeguards exist without compliance.
247 CMR 9.01(15) does not reach sterile preparations, complex non-sterile compounding, or non-sterile preparations that are not customary to the community needs.

Board Policy 2023-07 states its expectation of non-sterile compounding except for complex non-sterile compounding, and treats simple reconstitution of FDA approved, conventionally manufactured non-sterile drug products in accordance with manufacturer package insert instructions as not compounding.

247 CMR 9.19(24) disapplies the equipment and designated-area requirements of 247 CMR 9.19(1)(g) and (j) to institutional sterile compounding pharmacies, and 247 CMR 9.19(23) disapplies the designated-area requirement of 9.19(1)(j) to non-resident pharmacies.
247 CMR 9.01(4) and 247 CMR 9.01(16) each state no exception.

The telephone paragraph of M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 21 does not apply to an institutional pharmacy licensed pursuant to M.G.L. c. 112, s. 39I if the sterile drug preparation it compounded is to be administered to an individual admitted as an inpatient within the same hospital; the compounded drug preparation label is unaffected.

A pharmacy that is not both engaged in sterile or complex non-sterile compounding and licensed under M.G.L. c. 112, ss. 39G to 39I is outside the s. 21 telephone paragraph, but it still owes the compounded drug preparation label on every preparation it compounds, makes or formulates.

timing_deadlines.event: Revision of a USP chapter the licensee relies on
timing_deadlines.timeframe: No transition or grace period is stated; the duty runs to the most current standards
timing_deadlines.consequence: Once the revised standard is the most current one, working to the superseded version no longer satisfies 247 CMR 9.01(3).

timing_deadlines.event: Staffing of the s. 21 compounding pharmacy telephone line
timing_deadlines.timeframe: During regular hours of operation every day and not less than 56 hours per week
timing_deadlines.consequence: A covered pharmacy must meet both conditions, so a pharmacy with fewer than 56 regular hours a week still owes at least 56 hours of staffing.

timing_deadlines.event: Expiry of a Board waiver granted after June 30, 2013
timing_deadlines.timeframe: The fifth anniversary of the date it was granted
timing_deadlines.consequence: After expiration the pharmacy must comply with all regulatory requirements in 247 CMR unless the Board has granted a subsequent waiver.

timing_deadlines.timeframe: In anticipation of, or following, the expiration of a previously granted waiver
timing_deadlines.consequence: The subsequent petition must comply with, and meet the criteria in, 247 CMR 14.01(1) through (4).

forms_records.text: The container of every drug preparation compounded, made or formulated by a pharmacy licensed by the Board carries, affixed by the compounding pharmacy, a label notifying prescribed users and practitioners that the drug is either a sterile or non-sterile compounded drug preparation, in addition to the ordinary label elements.

For a pharmacy engaged in sterile or complex non-sterile compounding and licensed under M.G.L. c. 112, ss. 39G to 39I, the container also carries the number of the pharmacist telephone line, affixed alongside the compounded drug preparation label, unless the institutional inpatient exception applies.

A petition for waiver of a 247 CMR requirement is submitted on a form supplied by the Board, completed and signed by the current Manager of Record on behalf of a licensed pharmacy, or by the proposed Manager of Record on behalf of an applicant for a pharmacy license.

A completed waiver petition lists each requirement for which a waiver is requested with a brief explanation of why it should not apply to that pharmacy or pharmacy department, explains the compelling public interest and why adherence would be impractical and unduly burdensome, includes a comprehensive statement of the policies and procedures of the proposed operation with its safeguards for the public health, welfare and safety, and is accompanied by any additional information the Board determines.

247 CMR 9.01(15) requires no record of a refusal, of an extenuating circumstance or of a referral. Being able to describe and justify a circumstance relied on as extenuating is therefore the safe course, not a stated requirement.

247 CMR 9.01(4) creates no record, certificate or Board authorization of competence; it is satisfied by the pharmacist's actual education, training and experience and by the act's place within the recognized pharmacist scope of practice.

247 CMR 9.01(3) creates no Massachusetts form or record of its own. What it requires is adherence to the most current USP standards, so any documentation a chapter calls for is found in that chapter's text rather than in 247 CMR 9.00.

The patient profile a pharmacist and pharmacy must maintain under 247 CMR 9.16(7), a requirement that 247 CMR 9.16(8) disapplies to institutional sterile compounding pharmacies, is a record the Board's own regulations call confidential, and the safe course is to treat its contents as confidential information that 247 CMR 9.01(16) requires a licensee to protect; what the profile contains is taught with prospective drug review.

role_duties.duty: Practise pharmacy within the scope of his or her education, training, and experience and within the recognized pharmacist scope of practice, and decline an act that fails either limb whatever an employer directs.

Adhere to the most current standards established by each chapter of the United States Pharmacopeia, except on a point the Board has regulated otherwise, and work to a revised standard once it is the most current one.

role_duties.role: Retail sterile, retail complex non-sterile or institutional sterile compounding pharmacy
role_duties.duty: In the compounding its licence concerns, adhere to the most current standards established by USP, all chapters, and to the additional regulations the Board promulgates under subsection (c) of M.G.L. c. 112, s. 39G, 39H or 39I, as the case may be.
Not refuse to compound a simple or moderate non-sterile compounded preparation customary to the community needs, unless extenuating circumstances exist or the Board has granted a waiver.

Meet the expectation stated in Board Policy 2023-07, as guidance, that except for complex non-sterile compounding all pharmacies licensed by the Board engage in non-sterile compounding in accordance with Board regulations.

Maintain on the pharmacy premises the equipment necessary to perform simple and moderate non-sterile compounding and a designated compounding area for it, unless 247 CMR 9.19(23) or (24) disapplies the requirement or the Board has waived it under 247 CMR 14.01.

Complete and sign, on the Board's form, any petition to waive a 247 CMR requirement on behalf of the licensed pharmacy, or as proposed Manager of Record on behalf of an applicant, with the contents 247 CMR 14.01(3) requires.

Decide petitions for waiver: unless otherwise prohibited by law, the Board may waive a 247 CMR requirement if it finds a compelling public interest would be served, adherence would be impractical and unduly burdensome, and sufficient safeguards exist without compliance, and it may require the applicant to appear personally before acting.
Maintain patient confidentiality and protect a patient's confidential information, both against disclosure to recipients not entitled to it and against exposure in the pharmacy's ordinary workflow.

Maintain for each patient to whom a prescription is dispensed the confidential patient profile required by 247 CMR 9.16(7), a requirement that 247 CMR 9.16(8) disapplies to institutional sterile compounding pharmacies, and whose contents are taught with prospective drug review.

role_duties.role: Compounding pharmacy licensed by the Board
role_duties.duty: Affix to the container of every drug preparation it compounds, makes or formulates a label notifying prescribed users and practitioners that the drug is a sterile or non-sterile compounded drug preparation.

role_duties.role: Pharmacy engaged in sterile or complex non-sterile compounding and licensed under M.G.L. c. 112, ss. 39G to 39I
role_duties.duty: Provide a telephone number that fosters communication between patients in the commonwealth and a pharmacist employed by the pharmacy who has access to the patient's records, staffed during regular hours of operation every day and not less than 56 hours per week, and affix it to the drug's container alongside the compounded drug preparation label.

role_duties.role: Institutional sterile compounding pharmacy licensed under M.G.L. c. 112, s. 39I
role_duties.duty: Apply the telephone paragraph to its sterile preparations except one it compounded that is to be administered to an individual admitted as an inpatient within the same hospital, and label that preparation as a sterile compounded drug preparation all the same.

common_traps.text: Treating the recognized pharmacist scope of practice as enough. 247 CMR 9.01(4) also requires the act to be within the pharmacist's own education, training, and experience.
Treating training as an expansion of scope. However well trained, a pharmacist remains limited to the recognized pharmacist scope of practice.

Treating an employer's direction or a pharmacy protocol as authority under 247 CMR 9.01(4). The paragraph measures the pharmacist's own preparation and the recognized scope, and neither comes from a workplace instruction.
Keeping to the edition on the shelf. 247 CMR 9.01(3) requires the most current standards and gives no transition or grace period after a revision.
Treating USP as advisory where the Board is silent. 247 CMR 9.01(3) says shall adhere, and only a Board regulation on the point displaces it.

Reading the displacement words into a statute. For pharmacies licensed under M.G.L. c. 112, ss. 39G, 39H and 39I, adherence to the most current USP standards in the licensed compounding is statutory, and the regulations the Board makes for those pharmacies may not exempt them.

Attributing the National Formulary, or a revision timetable, to 247 CMR 9.01(3). The paragraph names the United States Pharmacopeia and its chapters and says most current, and nothing more on either point; the National Formulary appears in the statutory definition of USP in M.G.L. c. 112, s. 39D.
Treating compounding as an optional service. 247 CMR 9.01(15) forbids refusing a customary simple or moderate non-sterile preparation unless an exception applies.
Extending 247 CMR 9.01(15) to sterile preparations, complex non-sterile compounding, or preparations that are not customary to the community needs.
Treating a referral to another pharmacy, a preference or ordinary workload as satisfying 247 CMR 9.01(15), or as an extenuating circumstance.

Treating a waiver as something a pharmacy declares. Under 247 CMR 14.01 the Board may grant it, if it finds the stated conditions met, on a petition signed by the Manager of Record, and a waiver granted after June 30, 2013 expires on the fifth anniversary of its grant.

Assuming a pharmacy that does not plan to compound need keep no compounding equipment. 247 CMR 9.19(1)(g) and (j) require the equipment and a designated area for simple and moderate non-sterile compounding, subject to the disapplications in 9.19(23) and (24) and to any waiver the Board grants under 247 CMR 14.01.
Treating Board Policy 2023-07 as the regulation. It states an expectation and gives examples as guidance; the prohibition on refusing to compound is in 247 CMR 9.01(15).
Reducing 247 CMR 9.01(16) to a rule against telling people things. It also requires the licensee to protect confidential information, and exposure fails that duty without any disclosure.
Treating a secure channel, a transmission log or a requester's stated purpose as authority to disclose a patient's confidential information.
Limiting the s. 21 compounded-preparation label to sterile or complex preparations. It reaches all drug preparations compounded, made or formulated by a pharmacy licensed by the Board.

Reading the s. 21 inpatient exception as reaching the label, any inpatient, or any pharmacy. It disapplies only the telephone paragraph, for an institutional pharmacy licensed under M.G.L. c. 112, s. 39I and a sterile preparation it compounded that is to be administered to an inpatient within the same hospital.

Staffing the s. 21 telephone line only during regular hours when those hours come to fewer than 56 a week, or answering it with someone who cannot connect the caller with a pharmacist employed by the pharmacy who has access to the patient's records.
